title: Project: backup and rotation
goal: Build a backup tool that makes timestamped archives with checksums, keeps only the last N, proves that restore works, and fails loudly.
setup: # the data to back up: a database dump and uploaded files
printf '%s\n' '-- todo database dump' 'INSERT INTO todos VALUES (1, '"'"'buy milk'"'"', false);' 'INSERT INTO todos VALUES (2, '"'"'deploy v2'"'"', true);' > data/todo-db.sql
# P2: nine old backups (11 to 19 October)
# P3: the latest backup and its checksum
# P4: backups restored from S3 (file times are in the WRONG order) and a broken rotate script

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# (re)build rotation2/: 6 backups; the OLDEST name gets the NEWEST file time' 'rm -rf rotation2 && mkdir -p rotation2' 'for d in 11 12 13 14 15 16; do' '  f=rotation2/todo-db-202610$d-0230.tar.gz' '  tar -czf "$f" -C data .' '  (cd rotation2 && sha256sum "${f##*/}" > "${f##*/}.sha256")' '  touch -d "2026-10-20 12:$((30 - d))" "$f"' 'done' > make-rotation2.sh

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# Keep the 3 NEWEST backups (newest = latest date in the file name).' '# Delete the older backups AND their .sha256 files. Safe to run again.' 'cd rotation2 || exit 1' 'KEEP=3' 'ls -t todo-db-*.tar.gz | tail -n +$KEEP | xargs rm -v' > rotate.sh
# P6: a mock aws CLI (prints what it would do, does not upload)

warmup.q: How do you split an Nginx combined log line safely in awk?
warmup.a: At the double quotes: `awk -F'"'`. The request is field 2, status and bytes are in field 3.

warmup.q: How do you check a file against a saved checksum?
How do you stop two cron runs of a script from overlapping?
Why use `mktemp -d` for a restore test?
warmup.a: It gives a new, private, empty folder every run, so old files cannot hide a broken backup.

problems.title: A timestamped backup with a checksum
problems.situation: Every night at 02:30 the to-do database dump and uploads must be packed into one archive with the date in the name, plus a checksum file to detect damage later. For this exercise the time is fixed, so everyone gets the same names.
task: Set `STAMP=20261020-0230` (in real use: `STAMP=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M)`).
Pack the contents of `data` into `backups/todo-db-$STAMP.tar.gz` (use `-C data .`).
Write the checksum file next to it, from inside the `backups` folder.
Check the archive with `sha256sum -c` and list its contents.
hints: `tar -czf ARCHIVE -C data .` stores the files without the `data/` prefix.
`(cd backups && sha256sum NAME > NAME.sha256)`: the checksum file then has only the file name, not a path.
Sortable names: `todo-db-YYYYmmdd-HHMM.tar.gz`.

explanation.meaning: Date and time in the name, largest unit first, so names sort by time.
Go into `data` and pack `.`: paths inside start with `./`.
Subshell: the checksum file stores only the file name, so `sha256sum -c` works wherever the folder is copied.
Recompute and compare: `OK` means the archive is not damaged.

mistakes: Using `$(date)` in a file name: `Tue Oct 20 02:30:00 +0530 2026` has spaces and colons.
Creating the checksum with a path (`sha256sum backups/x.tar.gz`): after the files are moved, `sha256sum -c` cannot find them.
problems.interview_say: My backups use sortable timestamped names like `app-20261020-0230.tar.gz` and a `.sha256` next to each archive, so I can verify them before a restore.
problems.try_yourself: Use `tar -czf - -C data . | tee backups/x.tar.gz | sha256sum` to pack and hash in one pass. Compare the hash with `sha256sum backups/x.tar.gz`.

problems.title: Keep only the last N backups
problems.situation: The backup disk is filling up: there are 9 nightly backups and the policy is to keep the last 3. Because the names contain sortable dates, the user sorts by name (not by file time) and deletes everything except the newest 3, with their checksum files.
task: In `rotation/backups`, list the archives sorted by name.
Dry run: show which ones would be deleted with `head -n -3`.
Delete them and their `.sha256` files, printing each removed file.
List the folder again. Run the delete step once more: nothing must happen.
hints: `ls -1 todo-db-*.tar.gz | sort` = oldest first, because the date is in the name.
`head -n -3` (GNU) prints all lines except the last 3.
Loop with `while IFS= read -r f; do rm -v -- "$f" "$f.sha256"; done`.
solution: ls -1 todo-db-*.tar.gz | sort | head -n -"$KEEP" | while IFS= read -r f; do

explanation.meaning: Dates in the name make the order reliable, even after files are copied (copies change the file times).
Everything except the last 3 lines = everything except the 3 newest.
Remove the archive and its checksum; `--` ends options, so names starting with `-` are safe.
Idempotent: when only 3 are left, nothing more is deleted (Day 22).
`find backups -name '*.tar.gz' -mtime +7 -delete` keeps by age instead of by count.

mistakes: `ls -t` (by file time) after a restore from S3 or a copy: all files may have new times, so the wrong files are deleted (P4).
`tail -n +3` to keep 3 files: it starts at line 3, so it keeps only 2. Off-by-one.
Forgetting the `.sha256` files: they pile up forever.
problems.interview_say: I keep the last N backups by sorting the timestamped names and deleting all but the newest N with `head -n -N`. I do a dry run first, delete the checksum files too, and make sure a second run deletes nothing.

problems.title: Prove that restore works
problems.situation: A backup that cannot be restored is worthless. Every week the team restores the latest backup into a temp folder, verifies the checksum, and compares the files with the live data. The test must clean up after itself, and must fail if the archive is damaged.
task: Write `restore-test.sh ARCHIVE DATA_DIR` with `set -euo pipefail`.
Check the checksum first, then extract into `$(mktemp -d)` with `trap` cleanup.
Compare with `diff -r` and print `restore test PASSED` or fail.
Run it on `latest/todo-db-20261019-0230.tar.gz`. Then damage a copy of the archive and run it again.
hints: `(cd "$(dirname "$ARCHIVE")" && sha256sum -c --quiet "$(basename "$ARCHIVE").sha256")`
`trap 'rm -rf "$WORK"' EXIT` right after `WORK=$(mktemp -d)`.
Damage a copy: `cp` archive and checksum, then `printf 'x' >> copy.tar.gz`.
solution: echo "restore test FAILED: checksum does not match" >&2; exit 1
bash restore-test.sh latest/todo-db-20261019-0230.tar.gz data; echo "exit code: $?"
bash restore-test.sh broken/todo-db-20261019-0230.tar.gz data; echo "exit code: $?"

explanation.meaning: Do not even extract a damaged archive.
Print only failures.
A clean folder every time, always removed (Day 22).
Compare every file and folder; exit 1 on any difference.
The weekly job goes red, so someone looks at it.

exit code: 0
todo-db-20261019-0230.tar.gz: FAILED
sha256sum: WARNING: 1 computed checksum did NOT match
restore test FAILED: checksum does not match
exit code: 1
mistakes: Restoring into the live data folder to "test". A broken backup then also breaks production. Always restore into a temp folder.
Testing only that `tar -tzf` works. The files can be complete but old or wrong; compare with `diff -r` (or check row counts for databases).
problems.interview_say: I test restores regularly: verify the checksum, extract into a temp folder from mktemp, compare with diff, and fail the job if anything is different.
problems.try_yourself: Change one line in `data/todo-db.sql` and run the restore test again. What does diff show?

problems.title: Find the bug: the rotation deleted the wrong backups
problems.situation: After restoring the backup folder from S3, the team ran `rotate.sh`. It deleted the NEWEST backups and kept old ones, it left the checksum files behind, and the second run printed an error. Policy: keep the 3 newest by date in the name.
task: Look at the file times: `ls -lt --time-style=+%H:%M rotation2/*.tar.gz`. Compare with the dates in the names.
Run `bash rotate.sh`, then `ls rotation2`. Which backups survived? Run it a second time.
Find 4 bugs: sorting by time, the off-by-one, the checksum files, and `xargs` with no input.
Rebuild the test backups with `bash make-rotation2.sh`. Fix the script, run it twice, and check the result.
hints: `ls -t` sorts by file time, which changed during the restore. Sort the names instead.
To keep 3 with `tail`, the command must be `tail -n +4`. Easier: `head -n -3` on the oldest-first list.
`xargs -r` (no run if empty) or a `while read` loop.
solution: echo "--- left after the broken run ---"
ls rotation2 | grep -c sha256; ls rotation2/*.tar.gz
bash make-rotation2.sh                 # rebuild the 6 test backups
# Keep the 3 NEWEST backups (newest = latest date in the file name).
# Delete the older backups AND their .sha256 files. Safe to run again.
ls -1 todo-db-*.tar.gz | sort | head -n -"$KEEP" | while IFS= read -r f; do

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: after the S3 restore, the oldest backup had the newest file time, so `ls -t` put it first.
Bug 2: `tail -n +3` starts at line 3, so only 2 were kept.
Bug 3: the checksum files of deleted backups stayed.
Bug 4: with nothing to delete, `xargs rm` ran `rm` with no file. Use `xargs -r` or `while read`.
Rebuild the 6 test backups between the broken and the fixed run (the setup made this helper).

problems.title: Production-ready backup.sh
problems.situation: Put it all together in one tool for cron: `backup.sh -s SRC -d DEST [-k KEEP]`. It must stop on any error with a clear message, never run twice at once, keep the last KEEP backups, and print the crontab line to install it.
task: Options with getopts; `set -euo pipefail`; a `usage` function (exit 2).
Check that SRC is a folder; create DEST if needed; take a lock with `flock -n`.
Backup + checksum + rotation (from P1 and P2). Log each step with a time.
`trap` on ERR: print `BACKUP FAILED` with the line number.
Run 4 times with different `STAMP` values and `-k 2`, then once with a missing source.
hints: `STAMP=${STAMP:-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M)}` lets tests set the time.
`trap 'echo "BACKUP FAILED at line $LINENO" >&2' ERR`
Crontab line: `30 2 * * * /path/backup.sh -s /srv/data -d /backups -k 7 >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1`.
solution: usage() { echo "usage: backup.sh -s SRC -d DEST [-k KEEP]" >&2; exit 2; }
case $opt in s) SRC=$OPTARG ;; d) DEST=$OPTARG ;; k) KEEP=$OPTARG ;; *) usage ;; esac
[ -d "$SRC" ] || { echo "error: source $SRC is not a folder" >&2; exit 1; }
flock -n 9 || { echo "error: another backup is running" >&2; exit 1; }
ls -1 "$DEST"/*.tar.gz | sort | head -n -"$KEEP" | while IFS= read -r f; do
bash backup.sh -s nosuchdir -d nightly; echo "exit code: $?"

explanation.meaning: Runs when a command fails under `set -e`; `$LINENO` shows where.
Wrong options are a usage error, different from a backup failure (exit 1).
Lock file inside DEST: two backups of the same target never overlap (Day 22).
Real time in production, fixed time in tests.
Same safe rotation as P2.
Keep stdout and errors in a log file (Day 16).

problems.title: Copy backups off the server (S3, with a mock aws)
problems.situation: The backups must also go to an S3 bucket. The real `aws` CLI needs credentials and network, so here a mock `aws` prints the commands instead of running them. The user builds the upload loop and checks that only new files would be sent.
task: Put the mock first in PATH: `export PATH="$PWD/mockbin:$PATH"`. Check with `command -v aws`.
Upload every archive and checksum in `latest/` with `aws s3 cp ... --sse AES256`.
Show the `aws s3 sync` command that uploads only new files.
hints: `--sse AES256` asks S3 to encrypt the file at rest.
Use a bucket prefix by year and month: `s3://todo-backups/2026/10/`.
`aws s3 sync latest/ s3://... --exclude '*' --include '*.tar.gz*'`.
solution: for f in latest/*.tar.gz latest/*.sha256; do

explanation.meaning: A fake `aws` script found before the real one. Good for testing scripts without cloud access.
Upload one file.
Server-side encryption.
Upload only new or changed files.
In S3 itself, a lifecycle rule can delete or archive old backups (for example after 30 days).

problems.interview_say: Backups must leave the server: I upload them to S3 with encryption, using an IAM role instead of keys, and let an S3 lifecycle rule handle long-term retention.

problems.title: Rotation by age with find -mtime
problems.situation: Another team's policy is by age, not by count: "delete backups older than 7 days". The user practises it safely on a copy with real file dates.
task: Make a folder `aged` with 5 files dated 2, 5, 8, 12 and 30 days ago (`touch -d`).
List files older than 7 days with `find -mtime +7` (dry run).
Delete them with `-delete` and list what is left.
hints: `touch -d '8 days ago' file` sets the date.
`-mtime +7` = more than 7 full days.
Always the same find command, first `-print`, then `-delete`.

explanation.meaning: Create test files with old dates.
Modified more than 7 days ago (Day 12).
By age: simple, but if backups stop, all old ones still get deleted after 7 days. By count: always keeps N, even if they are old.

aged/backup-30d-old.tar.gz
aged/backup-8d-old.tar.gz
=== left ===

mistakes: Rotation by age when backups have been failing silently for 8 days: the job deletes the last good backups. Keep a minimum count too.
problems.interview_say: Rotation by age uses `find -mtime +N -delete`. Rotation by count is safer when backups might stop, because it always keeps the last N. Many teams combine both.
problems.try_yourself: Combine both rules: delete files older than 7 days, but never leave fewer than 3 files.

interview.q: What should a good backup script do?
interview.a: Timestamped archive, checksum, rotation (keep last N), off-server copy (for example S3), a lock against overlapping runs, stop on errors with an alert, and regular restore tests.

interview.q: How do you keep only the 7 newest backups?
interview.a: Sort the timestamped names and delete all but the last 7: `ls -1 backup-*.tgz | sort | head -n -7 | xargs -r rm --`. Or use `find -mtime` for age-based rotation.

interview.q: How do you know a backup can be restored?
interview.a: Test it: verify the checksum, extract into a temp folder, and compare with the source (`diff -r`), or restore a database dump into a test database. Do it regularly.
It sorts by file modification time, which changes when files are copied or restored. Dates in the file names are more reliable.
Not only on the same server or disk. Also in another place, like S3 with encryption and a lifecycle rule (the 3-2-1 idea: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 off-site).

recap.meaning: All but the newest N (by name)
Do not run if there is no input
Allow tests to set the time

recap.example: aws s3 cp x.tgz s3://bucket/2026/10/ --sse AES256
